title: ODIN and BAANG for Safer, Greener Skies
content:
Every time an aircraft takes off, thousands of structural components must work perfectly under stress, vibration and changing temperatures. Ensuring that these structures remain safe for decades is one of the greatest challenges in aviation. The COST Action Optimising Design for Inspection (ODIN) decided to rethink this challenge from the very beginning.

Instead of asking how aircraft should be inspected after they are built, ODIN focused on embedding inspection into the design itself. The idea is similar to the human nervous system. Just as your body feels pain and reacts early, ODIN worked on aircraft structures that can ‘feel’ damage and report it before it becomes serious.

As Action Chair, Dr Rhys Pullin, from Cardiff University, explains:

“Much like the human body’s nervous system, these ‘built-in senses’ will provide real-time updates on the health and safety of the aircraft. They’ll also help the plane automatically adjust its shape to improve fuel efficiency, make the ride smoother, and ensure everything is running at its best.”

Planes are struck by lightning about once a year, but this is always safe

Jet speeds have not changed much in decades

title: The future of early cancer detection with metamaterial technology and artificial intelligence
content:
Early detection and effective treatment of cancer are critical to improving patient survival outcomes. The rapid advancement of machine learning (ML), particularly deep learning, has led to significant improvements in the accuracy and efficiency of cancer screening, detection, and monitoring.

However, despite these advances, ML-based approaches face a significant limitation: the substantial computational resources required for the analysis and interpretation of medical images.

Detecting cancer at the earliest possible stage gives patients the best chance of successful treatment. Early diagnosis improves outcomes by enabling timely access to care and is therefore a critical public health strategy in all settings.

title: From overlooked disease to global research priority
content:
Every October, Breast Cancer Awareness Month brings people around the world together under the pink ribbon to raise awareness, encourage early detection, support patients and fund research.

To mark this year’s campaign, COST is publishing a success story about the LOBSTERPOT Action on lobular breast cancer. The aim of this research initiative is to improve the detection, treatment and outcomes for patients.

For years, invasive lobular cancer (ILC) was one of the least understood forms of breast cancer. Despite being the second most common type, research efforts were scattered and coordinated clinical approaches were limited.

To change this, the COST Action Lobular Breast Cancer: Discovery Science, Translational Goals, Clinical Impact (LOBSTERPOT) brought together researchers, clinicians, and patient advocates, establishing one of the world’s leading scientific communities dedicated to this disease. In the process, the network has launched new clinical trials, developed diagnostic guidance that could influence future global standards, and transformed the way ILC is studied and understood.

title: COST Action Blog: What is prayer?
content:
What is prayer?

This blog was written by the COST Action PRAYTICIPATE.

For centuries, prayer has played a central role in shaping worldviews, education and formation, religious experience, community life, and the organisation of everyday life across Europe. Yet, despite the “religious turn” in the humanities, prayer is still often treated as an ordinary or self-evident practice. This has limited our understanding of its complex and varied histories in the late medieval and early modern worlds. At the same time, the remarkable plurality of prayer practices is reflected in fragmented scholarship across disciplines and regions.

By approaching prayer as a participatory practice, social, communal, embodied, and mediated through material objects and media, the COST Action PRAYTICIPATE together with its strong international research network, seeks to develop a more comprehensive understanding of this widespread and multifaceted practice.

title: From policy to protection: making human rights count at sea
content:
From policy to protection: making human rights count at sea

As global attention increasingly shifts to the oceans for discussions or solutions for climate, trade, or conservation, the people who live and work at sea remain largely unseen.

Human rights do not stop at the shoreline. Yet for people who live, work, travel, or find themselves in distress at sea, securing those rights can become significantly harder.

Seafarers and fishers can face dangerous or exploitative working conditions. People intercepted at sea may be detained without clear legal safeguards. Passengers, scientists, offshore workers, and migrants can struggle to access medical assistance, or establish who is responsible for their safety. Distance and isolation make abuses harder to detect, while overlapping jurisdictions can make accountability difficult to secure. These abuses often go unnoticed and unpunished, also due to the vastness and isolation of the maritime environment.

title: Burden-EU: understanding the burden of disease
content:
Every breath we take contains tiny particles that are invisible to the naked eye and can harm our health. Air pollution alone contributes to heart disease, stroke, lung cancer, and other chronic illnesses. But how can we measure its real impact on people’s lives? How does it compare with other threats, such as smoking, diabetes or infectious diseases?

To answer these questions, scientists use a measure called the Disability-Adjusted Life Year (DALY). This combines years of life lost due to premature death with years lived with illness, showing how much of a population’s health is lost to specific diseases and risk factors. This helps governments to see the bigger picture and decide where to invest for the greatest health gains.

Before the launch of the COST Action European Burden of Disease Network (Burden-EU), each country used different methods, making comparisons almost impossible. The COST Action brought together almost 500 researchers from over 60 countries to create a shared framework for carrying out these studies. The result is more reliable, comparable data to inform policies that can save lives.

title: GoodBrother: not every brother is big
content:
On World Patient Safety Day, 17 September, we often think about preventing medical errors, infections or other risks in healthcare. But for older people living independently, safety can also mean knowing that help will arrive when something goes wrong, without giving up privacy, dignity or control.

This is where smart technology could make a difference. But it also raises an uncomfortable question: how much monitoring is too much?

The COST Action GoodBrother explored how cameras, microphones and artificial intelligence could support older people while respecting their fundamental right to privacy.

Imagine living alone in your eighties. A small camera could detect if you fall. A microphone could recognise signs of trouble and alert a carer. Smart technologies like these have enormous potential to help older people to live independently for longer.

But there is a problem. As soon as cameras and microphones enter the home, many people start to worry. Who can access the recordings? Who owns the data? Could helpful technology start to feel more like surveillance?

title: COST Actions at the 9th World One Health Congress
content:
The 9th World One Health Congress (WOHC2026) brought together researchers, policymakers and experts from around the world to explore the interconnected health of people, animals and the environment. Seven COST Actions showcased their work and brought their research networks into discussions on some of today’s most pressing One Health challenges.

The importance of the One Health approach has grown significantly in recent years as health challenges increasingly cross the boundaries between humans, animals and the environment. Antimicrobial resistance, emerging infectious diseases, climate change and other complex challenges demonstrate how closely these areas are interconnected and how difficult it can be to address them in isolation. Tackling these issues therefore requires international collaboration across disciplines and sectors, as well as the exchange of knowledge and expertise between different research communities.

title: When a little snout can LIFT the world
content:
Animal welfare is now well integrated in people’s minds and aims to make sure that animals are healthy, comfortable, well-fed, safe and able to express natural behaviors without unnecessary pain, fear or distress.

Animal welfare has traditionally focused on preventing suffering, with research emphasising negative experiences. Today, growing scientific interest and public expectations are shifting attention toward positive welfare, ensuring animals can also experience positive states. However, researchers have yet to agree on how to define or measure positive welfare, meaning no current farm animal welfare assessment includes direct animal-based indicators of positive experiences.

The COST Action LIFT will advance this emerging field through multidisciplinary research, cross-disciplinary knowledge sharing, training, and collaboration across Europe, helping lay the foundations for future progress in positive animal welfare research. Industry, government, NGOs, veterinary organisations, and farm advisory bodies are involved throughout the project to ensure practical solutions that strengthen animal welfare and support a more sustainable livestock sector.

title: AERoGELS: from airy ideas to real-world impact
content:
Aerogels are often described as ‘frozen smoke’ because these extremely light materials are composed mostly of air. Their tiny pores give them a very low weight, strong insulating properties, and a huge surface area compared to their size. They are widely used in construction, but their real potential extends much further. Through the COST Action Advanced Engineering and Research of aeroGels for Environment and Life Sciences (AERoGELS), researchers explored applications that were previously unknown, ranging from environmental uses to biomedical and food innovations.

The Action brought together scientists, engineers and industry experts who had never collaborated before. It created a strong European network that pushed aerogels into the spotlight with new discoveries, growing global recognition and ideas that reshaped the field.
